titolo: Why Britain's Slide Is Making Ireland Rich
descrizione:
For 200 years, the ferries between Ireland and Britain carried people out. Now the money is sailing the other way. How did Britain's poorer neighbor pull ahead, and how much of that wealth is real?

We follow the story on animated maps: famine, emigration, two Irish booms, Brexit, the Apple tax fight and the strange case of leprechaun economics, plus the weak spots that could turn the ferries around again.

scene.testo: A border where Brexit flipped the map. A tax fight where Ireland refused free money. A country twice as rich on paper. Is any of it real?
For 200 years, Irish ferries carried one main export: people. Four hundred fifty thousand left in the 1980s alone. Today, the money crosses the other way.
A magazine once called Ireland the poorest of the rich. The average Irish person produced under three quarters of what the average Brit did.
Now look at the same water today. Banks are moving staff from London to Dublin, and the biggest tech companies on Earth run Europe from this island.
On paper, Ireland now produces more than twice as much per person as the United Kingdom. But some economists say a big slice isn't really Irish.
So how did Britain's poorer neighbor overtake it? And how much of that new wealth is real? Start with the map.
Ireland is an island sitting behind another island. Between Ireland and the rest of Europe lies Britain, so for generations its trade went through Britain.
Even before Brexit, around 150,000 Irish truck trips a year still crossed Britain to reach the continent. Sometimes those trucks took days.
Its money was tied to Britain too. From 1826 until 1979, one Irish pound was worth exactly one British pound.
And its people kept leaving. In 1841, the island had almost 8.2 million people. Then the potato blight arrived.
Around a million died in the famine, and more than a million emigrated. The Republic wouldn't pass five million people again until 2022.
By the late 1980s, unemployment topped 16 percent, and government debt was over twice Britain's measured against the economy.
A third of the people leaving had a university degree. The country was exporting its brightest.
The odd part? Ireland and Britain joined the European club on the very same day, the first of January 1973. Only one looked rich.
So in the late 1980s, Ireland tried something drastic. It cut spending, kept taxes low, and went out to sell itself to companies.
It worked. Between 1995 and 2000, the economy grew by more than nine percent a year.
In 1997, Irish output per person passed Britain's for the first time. The same magazine now called Ireland Europe's shining light.
Then it blew up. Cheap credit poured into houses, and when the bubble burst in 2008, the government guaranteed every big Irish bank.
Their losses landed on taxpayers. In 2010, Ireland needed an 85 billion euro rescue from the EU and the IMF.
By 2012, unemployment was back near 16 percent, and young people were back on the ferries.
So the first Irish miracle ended in a crash. The second one needed something Ireland couldn't build alone, and it sat across the water.
There, in the most powerful financial city in Europe, Britain's model rested on three advantages.
One, the door. For any American or Asian company selling to Europe, Britain was the obvious first stop.
Same language, familiar law, and full access to the European market. Easy.
Two, the passport. A bank licensed in London could sell its services across the whole European Economic Area.
Banks operating in London held more than ten trillion euros in assets.
Three, rising pay. For decades, each generation of British workers earned more than the one before.
None of those three were guaranteed, and they started to crack one at a time.
The third cracked first. After 2008, British pay simply stopped growing.
One think tank estimates the typical worker now earns about 11,000 pounds a year less than if pay had kept growing at its old pace.
Then, in 2016, Britain voted to leave the European Union, and the door and the passport went with it.
Britain's own budget watchdog assumes the country ends up about four percent less productive than if it had stayed, with trade around 15 percent lower.
Before we follow the money across the Irish Sea, a quick ask. These videos take a long time to make, and subscribing really helps.
Take the door first. With Britain gone, Ireland became the biggest English-speaking country left in the European Union.

eventi.testo: Biggest English speaker left in EU

scene.testo: For an American company, it's the closest thing to Britain still inside the single market. And most of the giants were already here.
Google and Meta run Europe from Dublin. Apple's European base is in Cork. Microsoft, LinkedIn, TikTok and X all have big Irish operations.
They came for one number: twelve and a half percent. That's Ireland's tax on company profits.
It's now fifteen percent for the very largest firms, but Britain's main rate is twenty-five. That gap is the whole sales pitch.
Then the passport. The moment Britain left, a London license stopped working in Paris or Milan. Banks and insurers needed a new address inside the EU.
Dublin became the top destination. At least 135 financial firms moved business there because of Brexit.
Banks moved or plan to move over 900 billion pounds of assets out of Britain. That's about a tenth of the whole British banking system.
Roughly one in three fund managers that relocated chose Dublin. Even the trucks changed course.
Instead of crossing Britain and facing new checks, Irish exporters started sailing straight to France and Spain.
By 2021, a single southeastern port, Rosslare, ran 36 direct sailings a week to and from the continent.
All of this lands in one place, the tax office. In 2025, Ireland collected a record 33 billion euros in corporation tax.
It was the fifth record year in a row. So much that the government now saves it in two long-term funds.
Like an oil state putting away its windfall. Except Ireland has no oil.
And the people? Between 2016 and 2022, about 190,000 more people moved into Ireland than left. Same sea, same ferries, only now the money sails west.
But here's the strangest part. In 2016, the European Commission ruled that Apple had paid far too little tax in Ireland and told Ireland to collect 13 billion euros.
Most governments would have taken the money and thrown a party. Ireland went to court to refuse it.
For eight years, the Irish state fought alongside Apple for the right not to be paid. In 2024, it lost.
With interest, about 14 billion euros landed in Ireland's accounts. The government says it will go on housing, water, power and transport, not tax cuts.
Why fight that hard against free money? Because the money was never the point. The point was a promise.
Come to Ireland, and the rules won't change under your feet. Every multinational on the island was watching to see if that promise would hold.
So if this much rests on a handful of foreign companies, how much of Ireland's wealth is really Irish? In 2015, official growth hit 26 percent in a single year.
No economy really does that. Apple moved the rights to its patents and designs into its Irish company, and billions in profits suddenly counted as Irish output.
Nobody in Ireland got a raise. Economist Paul Krugman gave it a name: leprechaun economics.

eventi.descrizione: American economist, glasses, grey hair, suit

scene.testo: It got so distorted that Ireland made its own measure, modified GNI, to strip the multinational effects back out.
So let's use it. On that honest yardstick, Ireland sits about a fifth above the European average, and Britain just below it.
So yes, Ireland really is richer than Britain, just not twice as rich. Think a fifth to a quarter more, like a team that wins by a goal, not ten.

eventi.testo: Richer, but not twice as rich

scene.testo: And even that lead has weak spots. Ten companies pay almost 60 percent of all Irish corporation tax. Three of them pay almost half.
Medicines and chemicals make up around four fifths of everything Ireland sells to America.
So when Washington threatened tariffs on medicines in 2025, Irish drug exports to the United States jumped more than fivefold in a single month.
American buyers rushed to stock up before the deadline. A customer across the Atlantic can change everything overnight.
And the wealth hasn't reached everyone's front door. Housing is so expensive that one in eight Irish 25-year-olds has already emigrated.
In the year to April 2024, close to 70,000 people left, the most in almost a decade. More still arrive than leave, but the ferries never fully stopped.
But the best clue to what really happened is on the map. Look at the border inside Ireland.
Northern Ireland is part of the UK, but since Brexit it's the only place that can sell freely into both the British and European markets.
And since the Brexit vote, it has grown faster than any other region of the United Kingdom.
The only corner of Britain that kept a foot inside Europe is the corner growing fastest. So here's the scorecard for both of them.
Geography: Britain used to be Europe's bridge, and Ireland was stuck behind it. Brexit flipped the map. Now Ireland is the bridge.
Resources: neither has much under the ground. Both sell what sits on top of it: money, law and the English language.
History: centuries of one ruling the other, and a famine that began an exodus lasting over a hundred years.
Decisions: Britain chose to leave the club. Ireland chose to be the friendliest address inside it.
Ireland didn't overtake Britain by getting bigger or finding something in the ground. It stood on the right side of a line Britain drew for itself.
But that lead rests on a few companies, one tax promise, and an American customer that wants its factories back. If any of those moves, the ferries could turn around.
In 1988, Ireland was the poorest of the rich. Today it's among the richest countries on paper, and still clearly richer than Britain off it.
For 200 years, this sea carried people out of Ireland. Today, it carries money in.
Switzerland pulled off a similar trick, getting rich by selling trust to the world's money. That story is right here.
